fields.v: Adnan, B., Esposito, M., Taibi, D., Vaidhyanathan, K. (2026). Can AI Agents Generate Microservices? How Far are We? In: 2026 IEEE 23rd International Conference on Software Architecture (ICSA), pp. 13-24. https://doi.org/10.1109/ICSA66085.2026.00008. Read from arXiv:2603.09004v1 [cs.SE], 9 Mar 2026
Conference — 2026 IEEE 23rd International Conference on Software Architecture (ICSA), pp. 13-24, DOI 10.1109/ICSA66085.2026.00008 (from the IEEE export); full text read from arXiv:2603.09004v1
SERC, IIIT Hyderabad, India (Adnan, Vaidhyanathan); University of Oulu, Finland (Esposito, Taibi); University of Southern Denmark (Taibi) — academic

Evaluates; secondary: Compares — controlled empirical study of 144 AI-agent-generated microservices: 3 coding agents x 2 prompt strategies (P1 minimal, P2 with implementation summary) x 2 generation scenarios (Incremental, Clean State) x 4 projects x 3 microservices; functional correctness, code quality and efficiency

No SDD approach. Prompt strategies: P1 (microservice name + requirements path) and P2 (P1 + generated implementation summary). Scenarios: Incremental (existing system kept, target service directory removed) and Clean State (all traces of the service removed, generation from requirements alone). Agents (default settings and prompts, non-interactive, permission bypass): Claude Code + claude-sonnet-4-20250514; Codex + GPT-5 (high effort); Code Qwen + qwen3-coder-480b-a35b; agent versions not stated

Requirements specification document of each project (existing documentation); in P2 an implementation summary generated by Claude Code from code and requirements, with sections Functional Scope, Key Features Implemented, API Responsibilities, Data Responsibilities, Integrations, Technical Approach, Implementation Notes; role-based prompt templates (given verbatim)

Study flow, not an approach: (1) summary generation of the existing service (P2 only); (2) remove target service; (3) agent explores codebase or requirements, generates complete implementation, verifies compilation; (4) evaluation by tests and SonarQube
None during generation (non-interactive mode with permission bypass flags); authors conclude human oversight is still required for API contract compliance
Single artefact: requirements document (plus, in P2, a structured implementation summary) given as prompt context; no SDD workflow
Not classifiable (authors' wording: 'requirements specifications' and 'implementation summary' as context; no SDD terms)
Existing code bases: regenerating a removed microservice inside an existing microservice system (Incremental) or from requirements alone with all traces removed (Clean State, likened to greenfield)
fields.why: Incremental is clearly an existing code base. For Clean State the paper is inconsistent: p. 2 says agents work 'without any information of the system implementation' and likens it to greenfield, while p. 5 says only the target service's traces are removed from the system, so the other services seem to remain in the repository
fields.doubt: No Clean State só se removem os vestígios do serviço-alvo (p. 5), mas a p. 2 diz que o agente não tem informação da implementação. Decide se Clean State conta como new project ou existing code base.

fields.v: 4 evaluation projects + 1 pilot: PiggyMetrics (Java, 3 services), Train-Ticket (Java, 41 services), TeamSync (Java, 4), Project Management (Python, 4), MicroBank (Python, 4, pilot); 3 microservices regenerated per project; 144 generations; original code baseline about 982 SLOC on average per service (Fig. 3)
Microservice-based web systems (REST, Spring Boot): personal finance, train ticket booking, team collaboration/course registration, collaborative task management (banking for the pilot)
N/A (no participants; 2 open-source projects and 2 private student coursework projects)
Input and output tokens; monetary cost from API pricing ($ per microservice and total); generation time (minutes); measured from agent logs

Incremental: pass rate of the original unit tests of the target service (agents had access to these tests); Clean State: pass rate of integration tests of other microservices consuming the generated service's APIs
SLOC, Cyclomatic Complexity, Cognitive Complexity (SonarQube), as change from the human-written baseline

None (qualitative failure examples: structural package mismatch, prompt-induced configuration loss; Code Qwen produced no code in 3 P1 instances)

Automatic: Spring Boot Test (Java) and unittest (Python); SonarQube; agent logs for tokens, cost and time. Statistics: Anderson-Darling normality test (A2 = 20.068, p < 0.001), Wilcoxon signed-rank (P1 vs P2; scenarios), Dunn all-pairs post-hoc, alpha = 0.01

Average test pass rate over 4 projects (Table III), Incremental unit / Clean State integration. Baseline (original human code): Incremental 100 / 100 / 100 / 92.3 per project; Clean State 100 / 81.5 / 100 / 92.3. Claude Code + claude-sonnet-4: Inc-P1 73.7, Inc-P2 63.2, CS-P1 96.9, CS-P2 97.8. Codex + GPT-5 high: Inc-P1 75.9, Inc-P2 50.3, CS-P1 98.1, CS-P2 81.4. Code Qwen + qwen3-coder-480b: Inc-P1 50.5, Inc-P2 47.2, CS-P1 81.9, CS-P2 89.5. Cost per agent over all 4 configurations (48 runs, Table IV): Claude Code 7.8 min, $13.28/service ($637.39 total), 4,416K input / 2.1K output tokens; Codex 16.6 min (max 104 min), $5.92 ($284.19), 4,436K / 37.5K; Code Qwen 7.6 min, $2.98 ($143.08), 2,916K / 16.2K. Code quality: generated CycC 101.5-139.1 vs 146.3, CogC 66.6-81.9 vs 99.3, SLOC 713-920 vs 982 (Fig. 3; Claude Code and Codex 20-30% lower complexity). For every configuration: quality verdict no criterion stated by the authors; cost verdict no criterion stated by the authors

Projects: 4 microservice systems (2 open-source, 2 private to limit contamination), 3 services each removed one at a time. Configurations: 3 agents (each with its vendor model) x P1/P2 x Incremental/Clean State = 12 per service. Constant: prompt templates, default agent settings, non-interactive mode, similar network setting. Baseline: original human-written service. Acceptance tests: original unit tests (Incremental) and dependent-service integration tests (Clean State). Repetitions: one generation per condition (pilot observed similar outputs across runs). Human intervention: none. Pilot and summary generation done with Claude Code

Clean State gives higher pass rates than Incremental (mean +34 pp; Wilcoxon Z = 5.180, p < 0.001; Dunn confirms). P1 vs P2 not significant (Z = -1.475, p = 0.140), though P2 lowered Incremental averages (Claude Code 73.7 -> 63.2, Codex 75.9 -> 50.3). Codex best with P1 in both scenarios (75.9, 98.1); Code Qwen gains from P2 in Clean State (Train-Ticket 33.3 -> 97.0, +63.7 pp). Agent differences not tested statistically. Generated code 15-40% less complex than baseline. Code Qwen cheapest ($2.98), Claude Code most expensive ($13.28); Codex slowest (16.6 min). Better results on open-source than private projects (contamination suspected)

Distinguished scenarios (significant) but not prompt strategies; scenario difference partly reflects different test types (authors: 'evaluation methodology and context availability strongly shape perceived capability'). Repeatability not assessed (single run per condition). Limitations stated: unit vs integration tests validate different aspects; Claude Code used for pilot and summary generation may favour it; selection of microservices; network latency; prompt caching not accounted, so costs may be overstated

Threats: agent and parameter selection; generalisability beyond REST microservices; data contamination of open-source projects; different test strategies per scenario; Claude Code bias from pilot/summary; selection of services; latency; prompt caching not modelled. Gaps: architecture-specific benchmarks (diverse styles, explicit API contract specs, separate unit and integration tests, complexity levels); contamination detection; human-agent collaboration frameworks with intervention points and risk-based review checkpoints; architecture-specific agents and tooling

Replication package on Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.17863951: 144 generated implementations and prompts); not stated whether private projects are included. No pre-registration. Languages: Java (Spring Boot) and Python. Inconsistencies: abstract gives 6-16 min average generation vs Table IV 7.6-16.6 min; conclusion values garbled in the text ('6~5%', '9~5%'); Codex max 1.74 h vs 104 min (consistent); Dunn post-hoc reports the same Z = 5.180 as Wilcoxon; cost computed from API pricing for all agents, and the access method actually used per agent (bold in Table II: Subscription/API for Claude Code and Codex) is not recoverable from the text. Mapping of Fig. 3 values to agents not recoverable from the text. Lessons learned state that summaries 'degraded' incremental generation although P1 vs P2 was not significant

Partly (0.5): main conclusions follow and mixed results reported, but 'maintainable code' is inferred from size/complexity only, and lessons learned present P2 degradation despite non-significant prompt effect
fields.why: Judgement call: most conclusions follow and mixed results are reported, but 'maintainable code' rests on size/complexity metrics only and the lessons learned say P2 'degraded' incremental generation although P1 vs P2 was not significant (p = 0.140); another reader could score Yes
fields.doubt: As conclusões seguem os resultados, mas 'código manutenível' baseia-se só em SLOC e complexidade e a 'degradação' com P2 não é significativa (p = 0,140). Decide entre Partly e Yes.
